title: Orchard: An open framework for scalable agentic AI
gist: Microsoft Research open-sourced Orchard, a Kubernetes-native environment service plus three training recipes that let small open-weight agents be trained directly inside real deployment harnesses like Codex, OpenClaw and ZeroClaw. The headline result is Orchard-SWE hitting 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified (73.0% with value-model reranking) using only ~3B active parameters, approaching frontier systems more than 10x larger.

themes.theme: Open environment layer as the bottleneck

insights.claim: Microsoft Research argues the binding constraint on agentic AI progress is not model quality but access to proprietary sandboxes, closed training pipelines and private datasets that outside researchers cannot reproduce.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: If infrastructure is the moat rather than model weights, open-sourcing the environment layer directly erodes the advantage of closed labs.
insights.quote: Building state-of-the-art agentic systems often requires proprietary infrastructure, including custom sandboxes, closed training pipelines, and proprietary datasets that most researchers and practitioners cannot access or reproduce.
insights.locator: While there is excitement around agentic AI's capabilities

insights.claim: Orchard's core architectural bet is that the agent runtime environment should be a standalone reusable service rather than infrastructure embedded inside a specific training framework, decoupling environments from trainers.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: A standard environment-as-a-service layer would commoditize a piece of the agent stack that startups currently sell as a product.
insights.quote: The central idea behind Orchard is that the runtime environment should be a standalone, reusable service rather than infrastructure embedded inside a specific training framework.
insights.locator: Environment layer that scales across types of tasks

insights.claim: Orchard Env runs on Kubernetes to create, manage and remove thousands of isolated sandbox components in parallel, positioning container orchestration rather than specialized ML infrastructure as the substrate for agent training at scale.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Agent RL demand shows up as generic compute and container orchestration load, not just GPU load — relevant to cloud capacity forecasting.
insights.quote: Orchard Env’s Kubernetes foundation enables it to create, manage, and remove thousands of isolated components in parallel.
insights.locator: Environment layer that scales across types of tasks

insights.claim: A single Orchard environment service supports software-engineering, web-browsing and personal-assistant agents without modification, plus data distillation, RL rollouts and evaluation — collapsing what are usually three separate stacks into one.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Cross-domain reuse compresses the fixed cost of entering a new agent vertical, lowering barriers for small teams.
insights.locator: Unlike many existing frameworks, Orchard Env is designed

insights.claim: Existing open training tools cannot handle stateful multi-process agent harnesses, forcing researchers to train against a simplified stand-in and deploy in the real setting — a train/deploy mismatch Microsoft identifies as a core cause of weak open agents.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Naming the mismatch explicitly points to where open-model agent quality has been leaking, and to what closes the gap fastest.
insights.quote: Open training tools usually cannot handle these stateful, multi-process harnesses, forcing researchers to train on a simplified stand-in and then deploy in the real setting, which creates a mismatch.
insights.locator: Orchard also makes it possible to train agents inside any harness

insights.claim: Orchard closes the harness gap with a lightweight proxy that records the harness's own model calls as training data while each rollout runs in its own container, enabling end-to-end training inside unmodified deployment harnesses and across several of them at once.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: A proxy-based capture pattern makes any third-party harness a training environment — a repeatable technique competitors will adopt.
insights.locator: Orchard closes this gap: a lightweight proxy records

insights.claim: Training inside the real Codex harness lifted Orchard-Claw's success rate from 18.6% for the untrained model to 51.5%, a near-tripling that quantifies how much performance the simplified-environment shortcut was costing.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: A 2.8x lift from harness-native training means model benchmark scores alone badly misprice real agent capability.
insights.quote: under the Codex harness, for example, its success rate rises from 18.6% for the untrained model to 51.5% after Orchard training.
insights.locator: Because Orchard can train agents directly inside real deployment harnesses

insights.claim: Microsoft trained Orchard-Claw across ReACT, ZeroClaw, OpenClaw and Codex simultaneously rather than a single loop, treating multi-harness portability as an explicit training objective.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Multi-harness training weakens any single harness's lock-in over models — watch whether harness vendors respond by closing their interfaces.
insights.locator: Orchard-Claw is trained across several of them

insights.claim: Orchard-SWE reaches 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified and 73.0% with value-model reranking using a 35B-A3B model with roughly 3 billion active parameters, approaching frontier systems more than ten times larger.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Frontier-adjacent coding-agent quality at ~3B active params means serving cost for SWE automation could fall by an order of magnitude.
insights.locator: Orchard-SWE reaches 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified

insights.claim: The stepwise gains are disclosed: a 61.4% baseline rises to 69.1% with Balanced Adaptive Rollout, 69.7% with dense-reward techniques, and 73% with value-model reranking — showing post-training method, not scale, delivered ~11.6 points.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Method-driven double-digit gains at fixed parameter count argue that capability curves are still steep without new pretraining spend.
insights.locator: Together, these techniques take Orchard-SWE from a 61.4% baseline

insights.claim: Training used 107,000 distilled agent interactions from two open-weight models, MiniMax-M2.5 and Qwen3.5-397B, meaning a state-of-the-art open coding agent was bootstrapped without any closed frontier model in the data pipeline.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Open-to-open distillation removes the legal and dependency risk of training on proprietary API outputs — a durable structural advantage for open ecosystems.
insights.locator: we distilled 107,000 agent interactions

insights.claim: Credit-assignment supervised fine-tuning salvages the productive portions of failed agent attempts instead of discarding them, materially expanding usable training data from the same rollout budget.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Data-efficiency tricks like this reduce the rollout compute needed per capability point — a cost lever independent of hardware.
insights.quote: rather than discarding attempts where the agent failed to fully resolve an issue, the system learns from the productive portions of those partial attempts
insights.locator: The training process uses credit-assignment supervised fine-tuning

insights.claim: To fight sparse RL reward, Orchard adds a process reward model in which an AI judge rewards sound problem-solving behavior — reproducing the bug with tests, verifying the fix, checking for regressions — independent of whether hidden tests ultimately passed.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Rewarding process rather than outcome is how agent RL escapes sparse-signal stalls; expect this to spread to non-code domains.
insights.locator: Reinforcement learning comes next, but its feedback is sparse

insights.claim: A compact 4-billion-parameter value model trained on discarded trajectories from 20 prior experiments reranks candidate solutions at inference time, converting otherwise-wasted RL exhaust into a 3.3-point accuracy gain.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Test-time reranking is a cheap accuracy lever that trades a little inference compute for meaningful benchmark gains.
insights.locator: Finally, we train a value model on past rollouts

themes.theme: Data efficiency in GUI and assistant agents

insights.claim: Orchard-GUI trains a 4-billion-parameter vision-language browser agent on only 400 distilled demonstrations plus 2,200 open-ended tasks, yet averages 68.4% across WebVoyager (74.1%), Online-Mind2Web (67.0%) and DeepShop (64.0%).
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Strong web-agent performance from ~2,600 training items collapses the assumed data moat around GUI automation startups.
insights.locator: Orchard-GUI: A lightweight browser agent for real-world web tasks

insights.claim: Microsoft claims Orchard-GUI is the strongest open-source GUI agent while staying on par with proprietary systems from OpenAI and Google, an explicit claim of open/closed parity in browser automation.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Open parity in web agents pressures pricing for commercial browser-automation APIs.
insights.quote: making it the strongest open-source GUI agent while staying on par with proprietary systems from OpenAI and Google
insights.locator: Figure 1. Performance comparison

insights.claim: Orchard-Claw was trained on just 200 synthetic tasks and completes 59.6% of Claw-Eval productivity workflows within three attempts, rising to 73.9% when paired with the stronger ZeroClaw agent system.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: The 14-point swing from swapping harness alone shows agent product quality depends as much on scaffolding as on the model.
insights.locator: Orchard-Claw: Personal assistant agents for everyday productivity

insights.claim: The author draws the forward-looking inference that web agents can be scaled up without large volumes of manually created training data, implying human demonstration collection is not the gating cost for GUI automation.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Undercuts the thesis that human-labeled interaction data is a defensible asset in the agent stack.
insights.quote: The data efficiency demonstrated by Orchard-GUI suggests that larger-scale web agents could be trained without requiring large amounts of manually created training data.
insights.locator: Implications and the road ahead

themes.theme: Cumulative agent learning as the next frontier

insights.claim: Microsoft proposes treating RL trajectories as persistent assets distilled into reusable value models, so each agent generation inherits and extends prior experience rather than starting from scratch.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: If experience compounds across runs, accumulated trajectory archives become a real balance-sheet asset for AI labs.
insights.quote: Instead of discarding trajectories once a training run finishes, we treat them as persistent assets—for example, distilling them into reusable value models.
insights.locator: Looking ahead, we see reusing training experience

insights.claim: The stated payoff of open infrastructure is that teams no longer need custom isolated environments or proprietary cloud services to do agent research, an implicit challenge to paid sandbox and eval vendors.
insights.speaker: Microsoft Research
insights.so_what: Free, reusable sandboxing compresses the addressable market for commercial agent-eval and sandbox tooling.
insights.quote: Orchard’s results reinforce a broader point: the environment layer matters.
insights.locator: Implications and the road ahead
